text: Then Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD. This is what the LORD says: By this time tomorrow a measure of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria." [Footnote: A measure (Hebrew seah) was about seven liters of dry goods; a shekel was a weight of silver, roughly a laborer's wages for several days.]

versions.text: Then Elisha said, "Hear the word of the LORD. This is what the LORD says: By this time tomorrow a measure of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, at the gate of Samaria."
versions.explanation: A brief footnote on the seah and the shekel helps hearers grasp how remarkably cheap the food suddenly became, which is the whole point of the prophecy and its fulfillment in verses 16 and 18.

text: The officer on whose arm the king leaned answered the man of God, "Even if the LORD were to open windows in the heavens, could such a thing happen?" Elisha replied, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
Now there were four men with leprosy at the entrance of the gate, and they said to one another, "Why should we sit here until we die?

If we say, 'Let us go into the city,' the famine is in the city and we will die there. And if we stay here, we will die too. So come, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans. If they spare us, we live; if they kill us, we die.

versions.text: If we say, 'Let's go into the city,' the famine is there and we will die. And if we stay here, we will die. So come, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans. If they spare us, we live; if they kill us, we die."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew explicitly says the famine is "in the city" and that they will die "there"; the current wording drops the locative emphasis that sets up the parallel with "if we stay here." The fuller phrasing also reads more evenly aloud.

text: So they set out at dusk for the Aramean camp. But when they reached the edge of the camp, no one was there.

For the Lord had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, and they had said to one another, "Look, the king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to attack us!"
So they had fled at dusk, abandoning their tents, their horses, and their donkeys. They left the camp just as it was and ran for their lives.

When the men with leprosy came to the edge of the camp, they entered one of the tents, ate and drank, and carried off silver and gold and clothing, and went and hid it. Then they came back, entered another tent, took what was there, and hid that too.

Then they said to one another, "What we are doing is not right. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until morning light, we will be held guilty. Come, let us go and report this to the king's household."

So they went and called out to the gatekeeper of the city and told him, "We went to the Aramean camp, and there was no one there—not a sound of anyone—only the horses and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were."

versions.text: So they went and called out to the city gatekeepers and told them, "We went to the Aramean camp, and there was no one there—not a sound of anyone—only the horses and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the singular "gatekeeper of the city" here (the plural appears only in the following verse); the plural in this verse also forces "told them," which the Hebrew does have, but keeping the singular addressee is closer to the text and avoids confusion with verse 11.

text: The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported inside the palace.

The king got up in the night and said to his servants, "Let me tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the countryside, thinking, 'They will come out, and then we will take them alive and get into the city.'"

One of his servants answered, "Have some men take five of the horses that are left in the city. They will fare no worse than all the multitude of Israel left here—no worse than all the multitude of Israel who have already perished. Let us send them and see."
So they took two chariots with their horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army with the order, "Go and see."

They followed them as far as the Jordan, and found the whole road strewn with clothing and equipment that the Arameans had thrown away in their headlong flight. So the messengers returned and reported to the king.
Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans. So a measure of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, just as the LORD had said.
Now the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died—just as the man of God had said when the king came down to him.
It happened exactly as the man of God had told the king: "Two measures of barley will sell for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel, by this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria."

The officer had answered the man of God, "Even if the LORD were to open windows in the heavens, could such a thing happen?" And Elisha had replied, "You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it."
And that is exactly what happened to him: the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.
